CHAPTER I On Goods Considered in Themselves
Art. 79. Immovable goods are the land and everything incorporated into it naturally or artificially.
Art. 80. The following are considered immovable for legal purposes:
I - real rights over immovables and the actions that secure them;
II - the right to an opened succession.
Art. 81. The following do not lose the character of immovables:
I - buildings that, separated from the land but preserving their unity, are removed to another place;
II - materials provisionally separated from a building, to be reused in it.
Art. 82. Movable goods are those capable of their own movement, or of removal by external force, without alteration of their substance or of their economic and social purpose.
Art. 83. The following are considered movable for legal purposes:
I - energies that have economic value;
II - real rights over movable objects and the corresponding actions;
III - personal rights of a patrimonial character and the respective actions.
Art. 84. Materials intended for some construction, while not yet used, keep their quality of movables; those coming from the demolition of a building regain that quality.
Section III On Fungible and Consumable Goods
Art. 85. Fungible goods are movables that can be replaced by others of the same kind, quality and quantity.
Art. 86. Consumable goods are movable goods whose use entails the immediate destruction of their own substance, those intended for alienation also being considered as such.
Art. 87. Divisible goods are those that can be split without alteration of their substance, considerable reduction in value, or impairment of the use for which they are intended.
Art. 88. Naturally divisible goods may become indivisible by determination of law or by the will of the parties.
Section V On Singular and Collective Goods
Art. 89. Singular goods are those that, although gathered together, are considered by themselves, independently of the others.
Art. 90. A universality of fact is a plurality of singular goods which, belonging to the same person, have a unitary purpose.
Sole paragraph. The goods that form this universality may be the object of their own legal relations.
Art. 91. A universality of law is the complex of legal relations of a person endowed with economic value.
CHAPTER II On Goods Considered in Relation to One Another
Art. 92. Principal is the good that exists by itself, abstractly or concretely; accessory, the one whose existence presupposes that of the principal.
Art. 93. Appurtenances are goods which, not being integral parts, are intended, in a lasting way, for the use, service or embellishment of another.

Art. 94. Legal transactions concerning the principal good do not cover the appurtenances, unless the contrary results from the law, from the declaration of will, or from the circumstances of the case.
Art. 95. Although not yet separated from the principal good, fruits and products may be the object of a legal transaction.
Art. 96. Improvements may be voluptuary, useful or necessary.
§ 1 Voluptuary improvements are those of mere delight or recreation, which do not increase the habitual use of the good, even if they make it more pleasant or are of high value.
§ 2 Useful improvements are those that increase or facilitate the use of the good.
§ 3 Necessary improvements are those intended to preserve the good or to prevent its deterioration.
Art. 97. Improvements or additions that come to the good without the intervention of the owner, possessor or holder are not considered improvements.
Art. 98. Public goods are those of the national domain belonging to legal persons of domestic public law; all others are private, whatever the person to whom they belong.
I - those of common use of the people, such as rivers, seas, roads, streets and squares;

II - those of special use, such as buildings or land intended for the service or establishment of the federal, state, territorial or municipal administration, including those of their autonomous agencies;
III - the dominical goods, which constitute the patrimony of legal persons of public law, as the object of a personal or real right of each of these entities.
Sole paragraph. Unless the law provides otherwise, goods belonging to legal persons of public law that have been given a private law structure are considered dominical.
Art. 100. Public goods of common use of the people and those of special use are inalienable, while they keep their qualification, in the manner the law determines.
Art. 101. Dominical public goods may be alienated, subject to the requirements of the law.
Art. 102. Public goods are not subject to adverse possession.
Art. 103. The common use of public goods may be free or paid, as legally established by the entity to whose administration they belong.

The thesis opens with two general epigraphs and gives each development chapter a song, nine in all, under the method set out in section 2.6. They serve neither as ornament nor as authority and do not prove the argument. Each opening condenses, in artistic language, the movement the chapter carries out in legal language.
The epigraphs do not appear as ornament, nor as an authority substituting for scientific method, nor as empirical proof of the argument.<1>p. 73</1>
The argumentation is not founded on the excerpt, nor does it draw its chain of validation from it.<1>p. 74</1>
Each chapter opening condenses, in artistic language, the specific movement that the dogmatic development will carry out in legal language.<1>p. 77</1>

Platform governance is not exhausted by the written rule. It also runs through the design of screens, the language of the brand and continuous symbolic production. The curation of the epigraphs enters the method to grasp this register, made of anxiety, desire to belong, euphoria, frustration and capture.

The procedure is selective. Each song enters through the excerpt that matters to the chapter, without presuming total coincidence between the work and the problem, and the legal analysis does not rest on it.
In the platform economy, governance is not exhausted by the written rule.<1>p. 73</1>
It is also exercised through choice architecture, interface design, brand language, curation of affects and continuous symbolic production.<1>p. 73</1>

It is in this context that the curation of epigraphs is inserted into the method, as a way of grasping, in an artistic and culturally situated register, tensions constitutive of contemporary digital consumption, among them anxiety, desire for belonging, disorientation, euphoria, frustration, capture and performative compulsion.<1>p. 73</1>
Nor does the epigraphic curation import into the text the full content of the songs, nor does it presume total coincidence between the artistic work and the problem investigated.<1>p. 74</1>

In ancient Greek poetry, the Muses were invoked at the start of the tale to set the tone and place the voice that was going to speak. The nine songs play this role of frame, without claiming to be worth the same as the Muses. They also work as a chorus, which keeps the atmosphere of each conflict alive while the argument advances.
In archaic Greek literature, the invocation of the Muses, as in Hesiod, organizes the tale, delimits its tone and situates the voice that speaks.<1>p. 74</1>
The presence of nine epigraphs emulates the nine Muses and reinforces the framing character of the device.<1>p. 74</1>

In a dramatic key, the function also approaches that of the chorus, not because the text wants to theatricalize its object, but because it recognizes that certain conflicts require, beyond conceptual formulation, a voice that keeps their moral and affective atmosphere in circulation.<1>p. 74</1>

As a formal detail, the numerical coincidence between the nine Muses and the nine epigraphs of the work helps to make explicit, without any claim to equivalence of status, the function of the epigraphs as a narrative frame and a key of interpretive orientation.<1>p. 74</1>
Why are some in English and others in Portuguese?

The songs in English record the global grammar of digital consumption, with promises of belonging, incentives to exploit yourself and an opacity that seems normal. The Brazilian ones mark the return to the country's law and the passage from the problem to the answer.

The change of language has a function in the argument. The problem is born on a global scale, inside the platforms, and the legal containment is built with the Constitution and with the Brazilian Consumer Protection Code.

The anglophone block records the global grammar of digital consumption in its promises of belonging, in its incentives to self-exploitation, in its normalization of capture and in its diffuse regime of opacity.<1>p. 77</1>
The Brazilian block, in turn, signals the return to the institutional ground of national Law and the passage from the experience of the problem to the formulation of the answer.<1>p. 77</1>
The transition between languages is not a lateral aesthetic detail.<1>p. 77</1>
The problem emerges on a global scale, inside private platform architectures.<1>p. 77</1>
Legal containment, however, is built with national instruments, under the constitutional order and the Consumer Protection Code.<1>p. 77</1>

When technical architecture, formal terms and enforcement routines couple densely, the case ceases to be an “example” and begins to operate as a field of visibility, because it makes it possible to follow the passage between declared norm, norm in operation and disputed norm, without depending on abstract inferences or hasty generalizations.  <1>p. 56</1>

<1>2.4</1> On the empirical sources and collection techniques
It justifies the choice of the ecosystem by the density of the public traces it produces.

The <1>Riot Games</1> ecosystem, centered on <2>League of Legends</2>, was selected for the density and diversity of public traces it produces. The continuous operation of the service, the repeated administration of identity and reputation and the institutional presence of the game as a <3>p. 60</3> platform of participation generate abundant and heterogeneous empirical material, with user statements, records of conflicts and technical-normative documentation circulating in multiple layers. This availability is not treated as mere convenience, but as a methodological condition for articulating evidence about promises, relevant losses and mechanisms of private governance, in proportion to the argumentative weight of each statement, preventing the case from being reconstructed only from official terms or only from narratives of experience.  <4>p. 59-60</4>
<1>2.4.1</1> On situated institutional observation in a digital environment
It describes institutional observation and rules out ethnography and personal accounts as evidence.

Empirical collection incorporates a strand of situated institutional observation in a digital environment, intended to make observable the private governance that operates in the enjoyment of <1>p. 62</1> continuous digital services. It is not community ethnography, nor an account of personal experience as evidence. The procedure is employed to observe the platform as an institution in operation, that is, the mechanisms by which the offer is organized, the experience is conducted and the execution of the bond is carried out through technical artifacts, interface flows and instruments of sanction. This option responds to the core of the problem investigated, since the effective normativity of the ecosystem is not exhausted in the contract and does not manifest itself only as an explicit administrative decision either, as it is distributed through <2>design</2> choices, usage routines and operational procedures that structure access, value enjoyed and internal conditions of permanence.  <3>p. 61-62</3>
<1>2.4.2</1> On the documentary analysis of terms of use and internal policies
It presents the analysis of terms of use and policies as the capture of the ecosystem's declared norm.

Empirical collection includes a directed documentary analysis of the supplier's terms of use, licenses and internal policies, understood as institutional pieces that structure enjoyment and discipline the permanence of the bond in continuous digital services. The set of documents actually mobilized in the text is selected for pertinence to the problem investigated and has the function of capturing the declared norm of the ecosystem, that is, the repertoire of promises, duties, unilateral powers and enforcement procedures presented as a <1>p. 64</1> condition of access and use. In objects governed by platform, such pieces do not operate as simple informative accessories, since they take part in configuring the content of the supply over time and delimit, explicitly or implicitly, the range of admitted modulations, the regimes of sanction and the mechanisms of contestation and restoration.  <2>p. 63-64</2>
<1>2.4.3</1> On the survey of public user statements
It sets the subsidiary use of user statements, as a symptomatic record of frictions.

The survey of public user statements is part of empirical collection with a delimited and subsidiary purpose, as a symptomatic record of recurring frictions in the ecosystem. Its aim is to observe how controversies associated with enjoyment governed by platform emerge and circulate publicly, which losses are perceived and narrated, which expectations are stated as frustrated promises and which mechanisms of sanction, restriction or modulation appear as recurring triggers of conflict. This material is not mobilized as autonomous proof of the supplier's institutional conduct, nor as a substitute for official documents, interface records, lawsuits or decisions. It is employed to map recurring frictions, identify relevant vocabularies and discursive patterns and guide triangulation with the declared norm and the norm in operation, under minimal selection and recording criteria that allow external verification of the material actually cited.   <1>p. 66</1>
<1>2.5</1> On the procedures for reading and analyzing contractual terms
It explains why terms of use are read as pieces of governance, and not as a static declaration of will.

The institutional reading of the contract, in this work, starts from the recognition that terms of use and internal policies do not operate as static instruments for declaring will, but as pieces of a governance apparatus that integrates rule, implementation and continuous execution. In ecosystems governed by platform, the relevant promise is not exhausted in the contractual text, because it is reiterated and recalibrated by interface, reward routines, scarcity regimes and private sanctions. Even so, the contract remains legally central, since it is there that licenses, delimitations of access, unilateral powers and modulation clauses are articulated, which sustain the enclosure and administration of the bond. The procedure adopted consists of articulating the formal pieces with the evidence of institutional functioning in order to bring the case back to the categories of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption and make it legally decidable.  <1>p. 70</1>

It justifies the use of the epigraphs, because governance is also exercised through brand language and symbolic production.

The reading of the legal phenomenon of platforms refuses the artificial separation between norm, technique and culture. In the platform economy, governance is not exhausted by the written rule. It is also exercised through choice architecture, interface design, brand language, curation of affects and continuous symbolic production. Updates, events, campaigns, characters, <1>slogans</1> and performances do not surround the object investigated as mere ambience. They are part of its form of operation. It is in this context that the curation of epigraphs is inserted into the method, as a way of grasping, in an artistic and culturally situated register, tensions constitutive of contemporary digital consumption, among them anxiety, desire for belonging, disorientation, euphoria, frustration, capture and performative compulsion.  <2>p. 73</2>

<1>Technology, platforms and the techno-media economic order of digital consumption</1>
It opens the chapter with the shift of consumption to permanence in a governed environment.

Contemporary digital consumption can no longer be adequately understood as the simple acquisition of a thing or the contracting of a one-off service. In many ecosystems, the experience takes the form of permanence in a governed environment, in which the interface organizes access, induces choices, limits alternatives and distributes rewards or sanctions. The decisive shift occurs when mediation ceases to be perceived as a neutral channel and begins to operate as a form of organizing experience. In this regime, technique and media constitute practical ambiences: they frame the possible, define the relevant and stabilize certain conducts as normal through repetition, convenience and design.  <1>p. 83</1>
It links this environment to the economic architecture, in which platforms organize markets and extract value continuously.

This ambience is also inseparable from an economic architecture of its own. Digital platforms do not limit themselves to connecting users and offers. They organize markets, administer access, structure dependencies and convert circulation into continuous extraction of value. Infrastructure, data, interface and operating rules come to compose a single arrangement, in which the provision is prolonged, the bond is renewed by frictions and incentives, and the capture of attention and diffuse productivity is part of the ordinary functioning of the service. Economic rationality materializes in design, in curation and in execution protocols, so that competition comes to be disputed also through the control of ecosystems, exit costs and the administration of visibility.  <1>p. 83</1>
To describe this background without converting it into a mere sociological impression, three conceptual sets are mobilized, each with its own function. <1>p. 83</1>
From technique to the environment of life
First set, with the diagnosis of technique as environment and the critical key of Andrew Feenberg.

The first reconstructs the passage of technique and media from tools to environments of life, in which efficiency, automatism and integration act as criteria of social organization, without eliminating the institutional dispute over design and governance. On this axis, Jacques Ellul<1><2>28</2></1>, Neil Postman<3><4>29</4></3> <5>p. 84</5> and Willem H. Vanderburg<6><7>30</7></6> provide the diagnosis of the technical-media ambience, while Andrew Feenberg<8><9>31</9></8> introduces the critical key needed to rule out determinism and preserve the controllability of technical choices.   <10>p. 83-84</10>

The second set reconstructs the political economy of platforms as an arrangement of extraction, toll and dependence, in which digital infrastructures function as private territories for administering markets, coordinating supply and capturing distributed value. Yanis Varoufakis<1><2>32</2></1> and Ladislau Dowbor<3><4>33</4></3> offer the main lenses of this reconstruction, in dialogue with the critique of political economy and with categories of Karl Marx<5><6>34</6></5> mobilized to clarify the technical and economic form of extraction in digital environments.   <7>p. 84</7>
From political economy to the semiotics of consumption

The third set operates as a bridge between political economy and the semiotics of consumption, describing how value, belonging and recognition become organizing components of experience and practical conditions for stabilizing extraction. At this point, the anthropology of consumption, mobilized from Mary Douglas<1><2>35</2></1>, Baron Isherwood<3><4>36</4></3>, Arjun <5>p. 85</5> Appadurai<6><7>37</7></6>, Igor Kopytoff<8><9>38</9></8> and Grant McCraken<10><11>39</11></10>, makes it possible to understand that the objects consumed do not circulate only by utility or price, but through regimes of meaning that sustain bond, distinction and permanence.  <12>p. 84-85</12>

It opens the next chapter, taking the problem to the plane of signs and attention.

The techno-media economic order of digital consumption does not operate only as market structure, infrastructure and continuous extraction of value. It projects itself, with equal force, onto the plane of signs and attention, where value and delivery cease to be perceived as stable attributes of a “good” and come to be constituted by administered visibility, reputation, metrics and belonging. In platform ecosystems, enjoyment is not reduced to using a functionality. It involves participating in a governed symbolic grammar, in which prestige, rarity, recognition and experience are part of the content delivered as perceived, and in which the promise is fulfilled through reading codes and through equivalences built inside the environment.  <1>p. 261</1>
Umberto Eco · Guy Debord · Jean Baudrillard

To make this regime cognizable, semiotics is treated here as a material dimension of the legal problem, not as an interpretive ornament. The consumption promise stabilizes through signs, interfaces and regimes of representation that define what “counts” as delivery and which equivalences are socially recognized as value. In this key, the contribution of Umberto Eco<1><2>280</2></1> makes it possible to understand how codes and conventions make the provision legible and organize the consumer's expectation, while Guy Debord<3><4>281</4></3> makes explicit the centrality of spectacle and of the circulation of images in shaping desire and adherence. Jean Baudrillard<5><6>282</6></5> completes the axis by showing how, in attention economies, simulacrum and hyperreality shift the center of the commodity to its symbolic efficacy, making consumption present itself as access to experiences and positions, and not only as the acquisition of discrete utilities.  <7>p. 261</7>

The platform appears as an instance of private administration that organizes enjoyment through architecture, rules and <2>enforcement</2>, defining access, permanence and visibility. This includes both explicit decisions, such as policies and sanctions, and decisions embedded in <3>design</3>, in curation and in the metrics that select what will be seen, rewarded and reproduced. In this sense, governance is not an “accessory” of consumption, but an operational condition of the provision itself. The contribution of Julie E. Cohen<4><5>283</5></4> is mobilized to describe the platform as a form of organizing power that produces dependencies, structures conduct and naturalizes patterns of participation through technical and institutional means that are not exhausted in the contract.  <6>p. 262</6>

The asymmetry that matters, on this plane, is not exhausted in a deficit of available information. It forms as an inequality of codes and of language regimes that condition what can be perceived, compared and contested by the consumer within the environment. Luis Alberto Warat<1><2>284</2></1> and Maurizio Gnerre<3><4>285</4></3> are mobilized for this precise function, developing and fixing the perspective according to which vulnerability may stem from the difference between operational languages and languages of enjoyment, between vocabularies of promise and vocabularies of control, and between system metrics and expectations of experience. With this, semiotic vulnerability remains a structural category, linked to intelligibility and agency, and not an individual pathology or a mere absence of “enlightenment”.  <5>p. 262</5>
Samuel D. Warren II · Louis D. Brandeis · Byung-Chul Han · Eros Roberto Grau

The legal problem thickens when this governance assumes total effects over the consumer's presence and reputation within the ecosystem. The prudential reference of Samuel <1>p. 263</1> D. Warren II<2><3>286</3></2> and Louis D. Brandeis<4><5>287</5></4> is used as a methodological matrix for recalibrating categories in the face of technical mutations that reconfigure the field of incidence of rights and expectations, preventing the legal response from remaining tied to material analogies that no longer reach the real experience of enjoyment. Next, Byung-Chul Han<6><7>288</7></6> is mobilized to name psychopolitical dimensions of adherence and induced self-government, in which the bond is sustained by pressure of performance, comparison and continuous validation. Eros Roberto Grau<8><9>289</9></8> contributes to recognizing that normativity may operate as an effective order imposed by an organization endowed with power, making it possible to qualify as practical governance what presents itself as a “condition of use” or “internal rule”, but produces structural effects on ways of life and social positions in the digital environment.  <10>p. 262-263</10>

It qualifies the asymmetry as structural, semiotic and institutional.

In this context, the asymmetry between supplier and consumer is not only informational. It is structural, semiotic and institutional. It is structural because it stems from the concentrated control of infrastructure, rules and channels of visibility. It is semiotic because it bears on the production of the very codes of value, reputation and equivalence of delivery. It is institutional because it stabilizes through private procedures of adjudication, sanction and unilateral modulation, frequently opaque and with low contestability. The relevant vulnerability is not exhausted in a “lack of information”. It involves an asymmetry of intelligibility and agency in an environment in which the consumer depends, in order to enjoy and to exist socially, on grammars, metrics and access regimes administered by the supplier.  <1>p. 263</1>
It states the aim of the chapter, which is to make legally visible losses that do not appear as classic nonperformance.

The aim, here, is to make explicit how the capture of meaning and governed participation become constitutive components of continuous immaterial consumption, making legally visible losses and frictions that do not appear as classic nonperformance, but as degradation of enjoyment, lowering of perceived value and corrosion of belonging by <1>p. 264</1> technical and governance decisions. With this, semiotic vulnerability is stabilized as a structural asymmetry of intelligibility and agency in platform ecosystems, and the mechanisms are outlined by which enjoyment comes to depend on regimes of visibility, metrics and private sanction, to a degree sufficient to allow later legal qualification without depending on a demonstrative empirical narrative.  <2>p. 263-264</2>

It sets the normative basis, with the Constitution and the Consumer Protection Code at the center.

The normative basis mobilized is the constitutional order of consumer protection and of the economic order, which imposes limits on the exploitation of asymmetries, on structural opacity and on forms of exercise of private power capable of reorganizing access, information and risk. On this axis, the Consumer Protection Code is preserved as the central matrix of protection, while the legislation on intellectual property rights is mobilized with a functional status, as the legal grammar of access control and licensing which, in digital markets, structures the very form of circulation and enjoyment of utilities. Licenses and technical restrictions are not treated only as contractual content, but as legal-technological infrastructure that delimits what can be used, for how long, under what conditions and under which unilateral powers of modulation, without this operating as a generic authorization to degrade promises of adequacy, comparability and restoration in consumption.  <1>p. 54</1>

<1>On the legal regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC) under the Lex Plataformae</1>
It opens the chapter with the dogmatic task, which is to make protection operational without depending on material analogies.

The legal problem of continuous digital consumption requires parameters of qualification, evidence and attribution that do not depend on material analogies nor are limited to the contractual text. The dogmatic task is to make consumer protection operational in an environment in which enjoyment is modulated by private architecture, rules and <1>enforcement</1>, and unilateral alterations can degrade value and delivery without formally suppressing access.  <2>p. 391</2>
It links the Immaterial Object of Consumption to the immaterial product provided for in the law.

In this register, the reconstruction of the immaterial object of consumption is consolidated as a concretization of the “immaterial product” provided for in art. 3, §1, of the Consumer Protection Code<1><2>1</2></1>. The decisive point is that, in platform ecosystems, the object does not present itself as a stabilized thing, but as a bundle of functional and symbolic enjoyment that depends on regimes of access, visibility, updating and governance. For this reason, adequate protection requires recognizing two complementary dimensions. Functional integrity, linked to performance, to conditions of use and to the utility actually delivered. And symbolic integrity, linked to belonging, reputation, distinction and promises of identity mediated by signs and internal equivalences of the environment, when these elements are part of the provision as offered and perceived.  <3>p. 391</3>

The consumerist reconstruction of the IOC also requires a brake against the nominalism that separates “product” and “service” by label, without reaching the substance of governed enjoyment. In this sense, Rizzatto Nunes<1><2>402</2></1> is mobilized to sustain a sufficiently broad reading of the concept of product in the CDC, able to encompass border zones in continuous and mediated arrangements, without dissolving criteria. This broadening has no rhetorical function. It serves to preserve the incidence of the consumer regime when delivery takes place as a enjoyment bundle dependent on architecture, and not as an isolable material object.  <3>p. 391</3>
Karl Larenz · Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. · Humberto Ávila

Conceptual discipline and the intersubjective controllability of attributions are treated as a condition of validity of the proposed regime. Thus, Karl Larenz<1><2>403</2></1>, Tércio Sampaio Ferraz <3>p. 392</3> Jr.<4><5>404</5></4> and Humberto Ávila<6><7>405</7></6> are mobilized as methodological brakes to avoid elastic categories that explain everything and prove nothing, especially in matters relating to evidentiary difficulty and the objective confrontation of the technical opacity of platforms.   <8>p. 391-392</8>
Claudia Lima Marques · Ricardo Morishita Wada · Miguel Reale · Roberto Mangabeira Unger

On the same axis, Claudia Lima Marques<1><2>406</2></1> settles vulnerability as a structural datum of the consumer relationship and as an orientation of protection in lasting bonds; Ricardo Morishita Wada<3><4>407</4></3> prevents the illusion that volume of information restores autonomy, requiring qualified intelligibility, comparability and practical utility; Miguel Reale<5><6>408</6></5> offers the key of integration between facts, values and norms, making it possible to bring regularities of the technical environment back to legal categories without voluntarism; and Roberto Mangabeira Unger<7><8>409</8></7> enters punctually to offer a substrate of resistance to the institutional fatalism that confuses contingent arrangements with technical imperatives and to reinforce bringing governance by architecture back into the field of what proves amenable to protection by Law.   <9>p. 392</9>
It places the Lex Plataformae as practical normativity.

The <1>Lex Plataformae</1> is treated, here, as the contemporary form of practical normativity exercised by protocols, flows, interfaces, sanctions and private adjudication procedures that organize consumption in an environment. The consumer bond comes to be <2>p. 393</2> governed not only by clauses, but by design and by continuous execution, with structural asymmetries of contestation and evidence. This shifts the problem of abusiveness beyond the textual content of the contract and requires criteria capable of attributing liability for architectural decisions that lower enjoyment, alter equivalences and reorganize the consumer's experience without there being a traditionally identifiable “defect” in a product or service.  <3>p. 392-393</3>
It distinguishes legitimate alteration from the one that diverts the purpose of the provision.

In this sense, abusive teleology is stabilized as a controllable unlawful act of architecture. This is not an effort to prohibit changes, technical evolution or the necessary internal rebalancing of digital systems. The question is the recognition of the need to distinguish legitimate alteration, compatible with good faith, transparency and social function, from alteration that diverts the purpose of the provision and converts governance into a mechanism of extraction and unilateral recomposition of value, with a relevant lowering of the enjoyment bundle. Abusive teleology appears when technical, contractual or <1>enforcement</1> mutation reorganizes delivery so as to preserve the nominal existence of the object and, at the same time, degrade its functional or symbolic substance, exploiting the asymmetry of controllability and the consumer's dependence on the environment.  <2>p. 393</2>
It presents the two operational parameters, open auditability and functional value equivalence.

To allow institutional control and minimally intersubjective evidence, two operational parameters are then set. First, open auditability, characterized by the requirement of traceability and intelligibility of changes relevant to enjoyment, including with regard to access rules, modulations of delivery and sanction mechanisms, so as to make contestable what is produced by opaque systems. And, right after, functional value equivalence, as a criterion for assessing whether the alteration preserves the content delivered in terms of the promised utility and experience, preventing formal substitutions from serving to conceal substantial losses. These parameters function as grids of comparison to distinguish legitimate evolution from abusive practice, without requiring technical freezing or ignoring the dynamic nature of the object.  <1>p. 393</1>
It explains the place of intellectual property and of the economic order in the regime.

The dialogue with the legislative framework of intellectual property rights and with the Brazilian constitutional-economic order enters as a structural element of the regime, since exclusivities, interfaces and access regimes act as infrastructure of power and, for that reason, must be read under limits of good faith, transparency, social function and controllability. When enjoyment depends on proprietary grammars and on unilaterally administered conditions of access, exclusivity is not only a legal title. It becomes a condition of governance, with direct impact on the content delivered and on the consumer's position in the ecosystem. Legal control, therefore, needs to reach the way this infrastructure is used to modulate value, impose frictions, degrade equivalences and administer permanence.  <1>p. 393</1>
It states what the chapter delivers, which is an applicable regime.

<1>p. 394</1> The aim, in the end, is to deliver an applicable regime: criteria to qualify the IOC, identify the relevant injury in unilateral mutations and private sanctions, structure the proof of degradation of the enjoyment bundle and attribute abusiveness in a controllable key, with only illustrative and referenced use of examples from the empirical laboratory when indispensable to establishing intelligibility, with no autonomous demonstrative claim. This set prepares the conclusions and the guidelines of institutional protection, shifting the debate from “inevitable change” to verifiable standards of legitimacy in the governance of continuous consumption.  <2>p. 394</2>

It opens the next chapter by asking what kind of power operates over enjoyment.

Legal protection of continuous digital consumption requires more than the mechanical extension of consolidated categories to new realities. It requires identifying, with dogmatic precision, what kind of power operates when the enjoyment of an immaterial object depends on mutable private architecture, permanent curation and regimes of signs that organize perception, expectation and behavior. The problem can no longer be satisfactorily grasped by the classic grammar of product or service, conceived under assumptions of stability, one-off delivery and a defect knowable by relatively direct inspection. In platform ecosystems, experience is administered in flow, value is modulated over time and loss may arise not as an exceptional failure, but as an ordinary effect of design.  <1>p. 501</1>
It defines what semiotic vulnerability is and what it is not.

Thus, semiotic vulnerability is not to be confused with a psychological trait of the consumer, a generic synonym of digital fragility or a mere environmental description of networked life. It is a structural mechanism of power, bearing on the production of meaning, the intelligibility of the offer, the comparability between alternatives, the verifiability of enjoyment and the very conditions for contesting the loss. When the architecture of the environment organizes what can be perceived, promised, inferred and proven, the asymmetry ceases to reside only in missing information and begins to operate also in the form, the context and the regime of visibility in which that information appears. The central question is no longer only whether something was informed, but whether it could be understood, contrasted and effectively verified in terms compatible with consumer protection.  <1>p. 501</1>
It explains how what is naturalized as technical necessity returns to dogmatic language.

The proposed reconstruction starts from this mutation. Instead of accommodating the immaterial object of consumption to prior categories by hasty analogy, it seeks to bring back to controllable dogmatic language what is frequently naturalized as technical necessity, system rule or inevitable consequence of the infrastructure. With this, private choices of modulation, curation, opacity and sanction cease to figure as a neutral background of the consumer relationship and come to be examined as a qualifiable exercise of private economic power. The constitutional order, the Consumer Protection Code and the functional limits of intellectual property offer, together, the criteria for this bringing back, provided they are read in light of continued enjoyment, the functional integrity of the object and the centrality of the consumption environment as a space of normative incidence.  <1>p. 501</1>
It summarizes the shifts the chapter develops.

The stage now beginning thus develops a decisive shift: from the appearance of technical neutrality to the legal cognizability of design; from the mere making available of <1>p. 502</1> information to the requirement of legibility and verifiability; from abusiveness understood as an isolated episode to abusiveness incorporated into the purpose of the environment. It is along this path that both the need for criteria such as open auditability and functional value equivalence and the figure of abusive teleology become visible, understood as the incorporation, into the very operating logic of the object, of dynamics of inducement, extraction and normalization of losses. What is at stake is not only correcting peripheral excesses, but delimiting, in a constitutional and consumerist key, how far the private governance of the consumption experience may go when it comes to structure the very field of the possible for the consumer.  <2>p. 501-502</2>
